item.title: 20VC Trio EP.84 — Jensen's $1T Return / Anthropic's Record IPO With Insider Matt Murphy / "Vibe Coding Is Dead" vs Horizontal Agents (Muse vs HubSpot) / Cognition at $75B / Why Agents Are Stubborn / Mailchimp's 2021 Math (Conversational)
item.itunes:title: 20VC Trio EP.84 — Jensen's $1T Return / Anthropic's Record IPO With Insider Matt Murphy / "Vibe Coding Is Dead" vs Horizontal Agents (Muse vs HubSpot) / Cognition at $75B / Why Agents Are Stubborn / Mailchimp's 2021 Math (Conversational)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief 20VC Trio EP.84. Rory O'Driscoll is away, so Harry Stebbings and Jason Lemkin are joined by Matt Murphy of Menlo Ventures, an early Anthropic investor. Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia and the stock adds about $1 trillion, plus why the panel thinks his outside dealmaking gets reined in. Anthropic's $83 IPO, the largest ever, from inside the room: Google took 15 years to go from $10 billion to $100 billion, and Anthropic did it in one. Jason's warning that AI-driven hacking makes 2027 brutal for SaaS and vibe-coded apps ("vibe coding died about 90 days ago"), and why horizontal agents like Muse beat HubSpot for new small businesses. Cognition at $75 billion and the "number six player" bubble test. An investment committee on Databricks, Sierra and Ramp, and why "agents are stubborn". Deals: Palo Alto buys Applied Compute for $4.5 billion, Mailchimp sells for $3.68 billion after costing Intuit $12 billion, Bill.com goes to private equity, and CrowdStrike buys Zscaler. Also Claude and the Riemann hypothesis, OpenRouter and Chinese models, and what 6,000 Anthropic employees at $100 billion in revenue does to startup pay. Listen from 21:16 to 30:04, and from 37:02 to 40:54.
Listen verdict: SKIM-PLUS (~70 min with ads; ~63 min content). LISTEN `00:21:16`-`00:30:04` (AI cyberattacks, 'vibe coding died about 90 days ago', horizontal agents, Muse vs HubSpot) and `00:37:02`-`00:40:54` (Databricks as the place agents run; 'agents are stubborn'). Good: `00:30:04`-`00:34:30` (Cognition $75B; number-six-player bubble test), `00:44:37`-`00:50:28` (Mailchimp, 2021 2x question, Bill.com), `01:05:32`-`01:07:05` (startup pay vs 6,000 people at $100B), `00:13:48`-`00:17:33` (IPO day; Google 15 years vs Anthropic one). Skim: Jensen reactions `00:04:01`-`00:13:48`; stock worries `00:17:33`-`00:21:16`; CrowdStrike-Zscaler, Riemann, Chinese models `00:50:28`-`01:01:04`. Skip ads `00:01:17`-`00:03:57`, `01:07:12`-end.
Sticky insights: - Jason: 2027 will be 'the death of many SaaS players and vibe coding' because AI-driven hacking means you can't trust small apps; apps can self-maintain but 'cannot self secure'. - Jason: 'horizontal agents are what's gonna win next year' - a new small business has no system of record, so HubSpot's net new customers fell from ~10K to under 5K while Muse does the job in an hour. - 'Agents are stubborn': they leave instantly on price hikes, outages or breaches, and stay when it's cheap and it works - Jason's case for Databricks and Bill.com. - Matt Murphy: Google took 15 years to go from $10B to $100B; Anthropic did it in one - which makes Anthropic a 'troubling comp' for Cognition at $75B. - 6,000 Anthropic employees at $100B revenue means it can pay any cash comp; a startup that raised $5M after YC can't pay $600K engineers.

item.itunes:title: Big Technology — Is AI Racing Toward Disaster? With Tristan Harris: Am I Off the Hook? / Untrusted AI Watching AI / The Because-of-China Problem / Who Do You Trust With This Power / A 3–12 Month Warning (Conversational)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief Big Technology: Alex Kantrowitz with Tristan Harris (Center for Humane Technology, The Social Dilemma) on whether AI is racing toward disaster. Recorded October 14, so his proposed Trump–Xi meeting at APEC (Nov 17–18) has since passed. Why publishing the risks isn't the same as managing them ("am I off the hook?"), the Hugging Face incident by the numbers ($500,000 a day to review 50 petabytes) and untrusted AI watching AI, the OpenAI memo saying "we don't check under the hood anymore", and how distillation let China draft behind US labs. Alex pushes back: guardrails have mostly held (Anthropic's Mythos stayed private) and China is strong on its own merits. Then transhumanist incentives, the case for banning open-source models with dangerous bio capability, David Sacks' "why don't they just stop?", a Fed-style compute dial, and Tristan's claim that lab insiders expect recursive self-improvement in 3–12 months. Listen from 11:30 to 29:45 and from 1:00:10 to the end.
Listen verdict: LISTEN 00:11:34-00:17:47 (PDF line, Hugging Face numbers, untrusted AI watching AI, China distillation, 1,300 signers, naming and the third chapter), 00:20:25-00:22:52 (Daniel Selsam memo, 'don't check under the hood', poisoning, keyword collusion), 00:25:52-00:29:44 (Alex's guardrails pushback, GLM 5.3, French supermarket and Korean bank hacks) and 01:00:10-01:06:50 (3-12 month RSI, red line, APEC proposal, climate/nuclear winter, neuralese, Indus Waters). Good 00:05:02-00:10:05 and 00:46:38-00:53:45 (open-source bio ban, who to trust, David Sacks, compute allocation). Skim 00:31:05-00:42:48 (uploading, Munger, Ring of Power, Reykjavik) and 00:53:46-01:00:10 (government). item.itunes:title: How I AI — Claire Vo's 25-Task Benchmark: Gemini 4 Neon Wins / Coding Is a Tie / Fable 5.2's Narrow Lane / Opus 5.5 Loses Blind, Wins on Feel / The Claire Annoyance Bench (Conversational)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief How I AI: Claire Vo's solo model showdown, six frontier models (GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Neon and Carbon) run blind through her 25-task benchmark. Gemini 4 Neon wins on quality and cost, and it isn't close. Listen from 2:07 to 10:00 and 25:23 to 29:58.

item.itunes:title: Big Technology — The Shocking Return of Jensen Huang: Trump in the Board Meeting / Too Big to Fail / Handshake Deals and the Bank of Jensen / Best Case for US AI, Bad News for China AI / The Story Isn't Over (Conversational)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief Big Technology: Alex Kantrowitz's solo emergency episode on Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO, about a week after resigning over a series of sex scandals. How it happened: word that no national security laws were broken, a Sunday board meeting joined by President Trump, and Trump's "I gave them enough assurance." Why Alex calls Jensen "too big to fail" (Nvidia +32% in a day), Lloyd Blankfein's graveyard tweets, and the precedent for governance. The business problem underneath: handshake deals instead of contracts, the "bank of Jensen," no succession plan. Why this may be the best case for US AI and bad news for China AI (export controls, the Southeast Asia rental loophole, distillation), the SEC, FBI, DOJ and congressional probes, the New York Times report on Alice Wang, and Alex's prediction of a pardon. Listen from 3:30 to 11:30 and from 15:00 to 17:50.
Listen verdict: LISTEN 00:03:27-00:11:29 (no-national-security word, Trump at the Sunday board meeting, reinstatement + Trump statement, too big to fail, Blankfein, +32% day, why he resigned at all, 'enough assurance', precedent, structures that outlive you) and 00:14:55-00:17:50 (bank of Jensen, CoreWeave, handshake deals, is Nvidia well run). item.itunes:title: How I AI — Ankit Maheshwari (Innovaccer CTO): An OpenClaw Jarvis for Executives / Approvals on a Cron / Soul Files & Subagents / A Voice Agent That Calls You Back / Automate Every 1% Annoyance / Opus Bill vs GLM Flash (Conversational)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief How I AI: Claire Vo with Ankit Maheshwari, CTO of Innovaccer, on "Jarvis," the OpenClaw agent he still runs on a Mac Mini. It started with the approvals that made him the bottleneck (a cron every four hours for hiring, then Navan and Coupa), then grew into soul files with an orchestrator and scoped subagents, a separate voice-calling agent on Bland AI that books restaurants and phones coworkers who don't answer on Slack, lunch ordering that learned the curry-and-bread rule, a reverse-engineered smart home that turns on the AC before he gets home, and the "1% annoyance" rule. Plus the mid-flight moment it auto-approved team travel (and why guardrails matter), and why he's testing an open GLM Flash model against a $500-to-$600-a-month Anthropic bill. item.itunes:title: 20VC — Anjney Midha: AI Is an Energy Business / Stranded Power and Goodput / Fire the Bankers / Tranches as a House of Cards / Inference Is a Feature (Conversation)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief 20VC: Harry Stebbings with Anjney "Anj" Midha, one of Anthropic's earliest angel investors, recorded the day after Anthropic's IPO. Anj's case: frontier AI is an energy business ("buying megawatts and turning them into tokens"), the US has over 100 gigawatts of stranded power, and reinforcement learning can run on modular 5–10 MW pods plugged into it. Why on-demand compute at $12 an hour can beat a $3–4 lease once you price "goodput" (completed work). Then the rant: "glorified bankers" on Sand Hill Road, marks that "are not real," tranched rounds as a "house of cards" ("fire the bankers, bring in the scientists"). Plus: specialized chips 1000x more efficient for one stable model, Codex ultra-fast mode and monitoring agents from his phone, why enterprises will run local models (Mistral, Black Forest Labs, Red Hat for AI), Chinese labs locking up US clusters, his defense of Nvidia CFO Colette Kress, Elon as "a glorified compute reseller," and why inference is "a feature, not a standalone service." He does not answer the title's "Is Anthropic the real winner?" Listen from 5:00 to 18:00 and from 20:40 to 32:00.
Listen verdict: LISTEN 00:05:05-00:18:05 (energy business, Periodic superconductor, China 500 GW, 100 GW stranded power, RL on 5-10 MW pods, $12/hr vs $3-4 lease, Borg, goodput) and 00:20:40-00:27:10 (glorified bankers, marks not real, Harry's 'do they get a pass?', tranches + OpenRouter, fire the bankers). Good 00:27:10-00:35:55 (specialized chips, Codex ultra-fast, agents on the phone, local/sovereign models, Mistral/BFL/Cloud Act) and 00:47:20-00:53:15 (neoclouds + Elon, inference is a feature, Arena vs junk-food data, own your understanding). Skim 00:35:55-00:47:20 (pooling, China clusters, Jensen/Colette, tech as culture). Skip ads 00:01:24-00:04:26 and 00:53:22-end (box-transcript times).

item.itunes:title: 20VC — Kush Bavaria (Ornn): The State of Compute / GPU Landlords / Why Rental Prices Keep Rising / A Brent-Style Benchmark for Compute / Who Hedges (Conversation)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief 20VC: Harry Stebbings in the studio with Kush Bavaria, the 23-year-old co-founder and CEO of Ornn, which is building a financial market for AI compute (price indexes now, futures on GPU rental later). Kush's case: infrastructure investors are landlords who keep collecting rent as long as AI has tenants; GPU rental prices are rising, not falling; CoreWeave quotes late 2027 or early 2028; free renewal options have disappeared; and he wouldn't be surprised to see Nvidia's Rubin rent for $20 to $30 an hour versus about $7 to $8 today. He also gives the bear case: enterprises that never find a use for AI, defaults, and lenders stuck with chips. Then why compute needs a market: about 300 neoclouds selling nearly the same Nvidia GPU, a Brent-style benchmark built on one specific grade of compute, why Ornn had to go all the way down to controlling chips, and who will hedge (lenders exposed to neolab credit risk, and owners facing depreciation). Plus: his team runs on Grok Bot for daily tasks, Harry uses Instinct, Factory over Devin, why he picked a boutique VC over a big brand, hiring college athletes, and OpenAI over Anthropic "because they have more compute." Listen from 9:00 to 16:35 and from 28:58 to 43:50.

item.itunes:title: Big Technology — Aaron Levie: Why the Anthropic IPO Will Succeed / Everything Goes Code-Adjacent / Your Only Limit Is Compute / Frontier Plus Cheap Models / Answering Gary Marcus (Conversation)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief Big Technology's optimist episode for Anthropic's IPO week: Alex Kantrowitz talks with Box CEO Aaron Levie, two days after Gary Marcus made the bear case. Aaron argues everything is becoming code-adjacent, so coding's AI gains spread to cyber, manufacturing, legal and sales. He says knowledge work's time-in and value-out are now decoupled, so your only limit is how much compute you apply. Cheaper open-weight models and routing grow the pie: the frontier model orchestrates and cheap models (Aaron names Jev as one example) grind the bulk. From the S-1: revenue went from $1.4 billion to $17 billion in a year, customers paying $100K+ from 950 to 11,900, and revenue per compute dollar from 40 cents to $1.72. Also: Alex's breathing benchmark and why labs train where the money is. item.title: Lenny's — Tulsee Doshi (Google / Gemini): What It Actually Takes to Build Frontier Models — Snape's Potions Class, 60-20-20, First Evals, and Why Lenny Is Grok Botting (Conversational)
item.itunes:title: Lenny's — Tulsee Doshi (Google / Gemini): What It Actually Takes to Build Frontier Models — Snape's Potions Class, 60-20-20, First Evals, and Why Lenny Is Grok Botting (Conversational)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief Lenny's Podcast with Tulsee Doshi, head of product for Google's frontier AI models (Gemini, plus GenMedia models such as Nano Banana and Lyria, Gemma, and Gemini audio): why model development is like Snape's potions class — you set goals and evals, but the model isn't predictable, so a research PM has to notice where it uniquely shines; Google's full-stack strategy and Gemini 4 Argon; chain-of-thought monitors and partnering with Wiz (now a Google company) on Scan for Good; why the model itself has a UX; "PM ascendance" and the skills that matter (vibes, writing your first eval from five prompts, adaptability); improving skin-tone representation with the Monk ten-tone scale; evaluating the full served experience; Stanford flash teams mapped onto agent swarms; the 60-20-20 rule and what a harness actually is; upskilling PMs (shared skills, a two-day November workshop, "if you have to do something twice"); Lenny's habit of asking "can AI do this for me?" while "Grok Botting," and his list of Grok Bot, Muse, Instinct, and Dots as assistants already using Google data; burnout, avoiding AI slop (insight from you, data from the model); and how the PM job now needs heft past a requirements doc.
Listen verdict: LISTEN if you care about how a frontier lab runs product, or about personal AI assistants — Lenny names Grok Bot, Instinct, Muse, and Dots on air (41:18–44:10). Otherwise SKIM: potions-class model building 01:08–05:29 · strategy + safety 06:28–14:10 · form factors + model-as-UX + PM ascendance 14:10–23:04 · first eval, vibes, skin-tone and end-to-end evals 23:04–29:49 · flash teams 30:38–33:13 · 60-20-20 + adaptability + harness 33:13–37:30 · upskilling + “can AI do this?” + personal assistant 37:30–44:10 · burnout + slop + PM-role change 44:10–51:02. Lightning worth a dip: Wispr Flow 53:33–54:04 · serendipity motto 54:11–55:31 · dance / India Festival / seven-month-old 55:31–57:02 · Rambler on Gboard 57:14–58:00. Skip teaser 00:00–01:08, WorkOS 05:29–06:25, DX 29:49–30:36.
Sticky insights: - Model development is like Snape's potions class: set goals and evals, monitor the run scientifically, and still expect surprising magic — a research PM has to notice where the finished model uniquely shines - 60-20-20: about 60% of what you build should work now, 20% is rough but near, 20% is a glimmer of a magical experience; 'build three months ahead' is hard even from inside the model team - First eval: start with five prompts, get to about 20 that separate model A from model B, and rate them yourself before you scale; evaluate the whole served experience, not just the raw model - A harness is the wrapper around the model (system instructions, tools, skills, context, environment); rigid harnesses get eaten for breakfast as models improve — retest, or even delete skills and see (Boris Cherny, via Lenny) - Lenny is 'doing a lot of Grok Botting' and lists Grok Bot, Muse, Instinct, and Dots as personal assistants already doing magical things with Gmail/Calendar/Docs; Google, he says, has not yet shipped something people get really excited about (Spark is 'trying'). Tulsee: stay tuned / more work to do

item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief Moonshots #309, "The Great Collision Between Politics and AI," recorded the day after the 2026 midterms. Peter is away, so Salim Ismail hosts Dave Blundin and Alex Wissner-Gross. Muse and Dot get one passing mention; Grok Bot, Instinct and Town are not named. Listen from 38:40 to 47:50 and from 1:10:40 to 1:23:40.

item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief Lenny's Podcast with Hector Serrano, Head of Content at Wispr Flow, who joined at 19 as an intern: why the product (not a hack) drove growth and why to turn paid ads on early as a learning tool; the organic UGC program that hit ~500M views and got killed for not converting; the performance-paid creator model on Trybe (a cut of ad spend for SaaS, of sales for e-com), the "smart retainer" floor, and creators earning ~$13K a month with 1–2K followers; building a 50-creator roster step by step (150–250 hand-written DMs → 5–6 creators, culture, slow growth, Meta's 60% similarity grouping and the rain-keyboard ad); ugly ads for technical buyers; the onboarding call; a ~15-person flat marketing team and why an ad now dies at ~$100K spend; hiring hungry young talent over resumes; "the best marketers are allergic to AI"; founder-led content and why YouTube packaging beats production; plus Miso, and Hector's one Instinct comparison.

item.description: Andrew and Ava brief Moonshots #307 with Peter Diamandis, Salim Ismail, Dave Blundin, Alex Wissner-Gross and guest Emad Mostaque: why Alphabet had its worst stock day ever (down 13%, about $500B) despite a billion Gemini users, 25% revenue growth and a doubled cloud business; Gemini 4 Carbon's benchmark jump and Alex's "big asterisk"; Emad's call that search advertising tops out in Q1 because the assistant closest to you does the buying (and people use Dots and Grok Bot, "a million users," not Gemini Spark); Intel down 28% and the CPU-bottleneck debate; Sam Altman's "hold my beer" channel, about $10M for a Navier-Stokes result, and OpenAI's robots for self-replicating data centers; Optimus coming off the Fremont line and who buys a million robots; Tesla vs Waymo on cost per mile and Emad's 40,000-Cybercab math; Cambridge Teamsters vs driverless taxis; the CS and MBA enrollment slump; Anduril's Blue Chip laptop; and an AMA on switching models, Chinese model pricing and "the markup on the markup on the markup."
